newsitem.title: UK: Thatcher "hugely disappointed" by UK election.
newsitem.headline: Thatcher "hugely disappointed" by UK election.

text.p: Margaret Thatcher, whose premiership transformed the face of Britain, was said on Friday to be "hugely disappointed" by Labour's landslide victory spelling the end of an era she dominated.

Thatcher, who had condemned her successor John Major with faint praise but then canvassed in his support, watched the results deep into the night on television, her press secretary Elizabeth Buchanan said.

"She is hugely disappointed. She has no plans to make any further statement. She stayed up late into the night watching the results. But she is now busy working on her preparations for a lecture tour in the United States next week."
Labour leader Tony Blair has made no secret of his admiration for the forceful "Iron Lady", saying: "She was a thoroughly determined person and that is an admirable quality."

Blair, who dragged his own party into the middle ground of British politics and dumped much of its socialist dogma in his triumphant bid to end 18 years in the political wilderness, even called himself her natural heir.
He said that only the new-look Labour Party was capable of completing the "economic and social revolution" she began.
That provoked the frosty response from Thatcher: "He is trying to take over my policies."
Thatcher has called Blair "the most formidable" Labour leader of the past 30 years but dismissed those who saw any reflection in him of her conviction politics and charisma.
"I think they have got the sex wrong. I think they have got the willpower wrong. I think they have got the reasoning wrong. I think they have got the strength wrong," she said.
After winning three elections in a row, Thatcher was bundled out of office in 1990 by her Conservative colleagues who felt that her hectoring tone and autocratic ways made her unelectable.
In her 11 years in office, she privatised state industries, crushed the power of the trade unions and went to war with Argentina to liberate the Falkland Islands.

John Major was the chosen heir of Britain's longest-serving premier of the 20th century but she constantly sniped at him from the sidelines, saying that he never seized the big ideas and "drifted with the tide".
In her only interview of the current campaign, the workaholic Thatcher confessed that seven years after her departure from Downing Street it was still difficult to let go.
"I got so used to being in charge that it takes a long time to get out of an old habit," she told the Sunday Telegraph.
But the redoutable 71-year-old insisted: "I have no wish to come back. Now I am free to roam the world and preach my beliefs -- and I am having an effect."
Thatcher, who crusades for a free market through her own institute and international lecture tours, was critical of the statutory six-week election campaign.
"Three weeks (of campaigning) is quite long enough, otherwise people get bored. And anyway, it's the last week that counts. That's when you can really change things," she said.
